etymology: A city in the hill country of Judah, afterward set apart to the priests, the sons of Aaron; called Hilen in the Chronicler’s list. The name is taken to mean “sandy” or “strong place.”
biblical_def: Holon is a city in the hill country of Judah, numbered among the towns of Judah’s inheritance: “And Goshen, and Holon, and Giloh; eleven cities with their villages” (Jos 15:51). When the land was portioned out, Holon was drawn from Judah’s allotment and given to the sons of Aaron the priest as one of the cities with suburbs: “And Holon with her suburbs, and Debir with her suburbs” (Jos 21:15). The Chronicler names the same city Hilen (1Ch 6:58). Here is a small but weighty thing: the priests received no continuous territory of their own, for the LORD had said to Aaron, “I am thy part and thine inheritance among the children of Israel” (Num 18:20). Their portion was scattered through the tribes in towns like Holon, that the ministers of holy things might dwell in every quarter of the land, near to the people they served. So an obscure hill-town becomes a parable of the ministry: the servants of God own little of earth, for God Himself is their inheritance, and they are set among the people to teach the law and offer the sacrifices. The believer today, a priest unto God in Christ, learns the same lesson at Holon — that his treasure is not in acres but in the LORD who is his portion for ever.

etymology: A city in the hill country of Judah near Hebron, named in the roll of Judah’s inheritance; the name is taken to mean “ambush” or “lurking-place.” Not to be confounded with the Arab peoples.
biblical_def: Arab is a city in the hill country of Judah, set down in a single verse of the great catalogue of Judah’s towns: “Arab, and Dumah, and Eshean” (Jos 15:52). It appears among the cities of the mountains near Hebron, and no further story is told of it in all the Scripture. Yet its bare naming is itself a testimony. When the LORD apportioned Canaan to His people, He did not deal in vague promises of “a land” but numbered the very towns, one by one, down to the least hamlet of the hills, that Israel might know the exactness of God’s faithfulness. “And the LORD gave unto Israel all the land which he sware to give unto their fathers; and they possessed it, and dwelt therein” (Jos 21:43). Arab is one grain in that harvest of promise kept. The name is thought to mean an ambush or lurking-place, a rough hill-country hold; but under the hand of God it became a dwelling of His covenant people. Let no believer despise the small and unrecorded places of God’s dealings. The God who wrote Arab into His book by name is the God who has the very hairs of your head numbered, and who forgets not the least of those whom He has given to His Son.

etymology: A city in the hill country of Judah, named in the roll of Judah’s inheritance; the name means “silence” or “stillness.” The same name is borne by an oracle against Edom in Isaiah, whence the watchman’s cry.
biblical_def: Dumah is a city in the hill country of Judah, listed with its neighbors in the great roll of Judah’s towns: “Arab, and Dumah, and Eshean” (Jos 15:52). The name means silence or stillness. The prophet Isaiah takes up the same word in his burden against Edom and Arabia: “The burden of Dumah. He calleth to me out of Seir, Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” (Isa 21:11). There the silent name becomes the setting for one of Scripture’s great questions — a voice crying out of the darkness to the watchman, asking how far spent the night is, whether morning comes. The watchman answers, “The morning cometh, and also the night” (Isa 21:12): for the ungodly there is a fleeting light and then the deeper dark, but for the people of God the true morning surely dawns. So the little hill-town of Silence points, by its very name, to the whole posture of the watchful believer, who waits through the long night of this age and cries to know when the day will break. The Christian is set as such a watchman, called to sober vigilance until the Sun of Righteousness arise with healing in His wings, and the shadows flee away.

etymology: A city in the hill country of Judah near Hebron, named in the roll of Judah’s inheritance; the name is taken to mean “smallness” or “littleness.”
biblical_def: Zior is a city in the hill country of Judah, closing a short cluster of towns near Hebron: “And Humtah, and Kirjatharba, which is Hebron, and Zior; nine cities with their villages” (Jos 15:54). It is named but once, and its very name is thought to mean smallness or littleness. So the last town in the list is the little one, and it too is written into the book of the inheritance and numbered among the nine. When God portioned the land, He did not pass over the small place because it was small. The mighty Hebron, city of Abraham and of the patriarchs’ graves, and little Zior stand side by side in one verse, both given by the same faithful hand: “There failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken unto the house of Israel; all came to pass” (Jos 21:45). This is the way of God throughout Scripture — He has chosen the small things, the base things, the things which are not, to bring to nought the things that are, that no flesh should glory in His presence. The believer who feels himself a Zior, little and unregarded among the towns of men, may take heart: the God of the inheritance forgets no small place, and writes the littlest name in His book with the same steadfast faithfulness as the great.

etymology: The name of two cities in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, both named in the roll of Judah’s inheritance; the name is taken to mean “strong” or “a strong place.”
biblical_def: Ashnah is the name of two distinct cities in the lowland of Judah, the rolling foothills between the hill country and the Philistine plain. The first stands near the head of the lowland list: “And in the valley, Eshtaol, and Zoreah, and Ashnah” (Jos 15:33). The second appears further down the same catalogue: “And Jiphtah, and Ashnah, and Nezib” (Jos 15:43). That two towns bore the same name, both meaning strength or a strong place, tells of the character of the Shephelah — a borderland of walled towns and fortified holds, the shield of Judah against the Philistine. Yet the strength of these places was never in their walls. The Shephelah was ground fought over again and again, and Judah held it only as the LORD was her strength. “The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped” (Psa 28:7). The two Ashnahs preach, by their very name, the lesson Judah so often forgot and so dearly relearned: that a strong place is no defence when the LORD departs, and the weakest hold is safe when He is its wall of fire round about. The believer’s stronghold is not his own resolve or circumstance, but the name of the LORD, which is a strong tower into which the righteous runneth and is safe.

etymology: A city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, named in the roll of Judah’s inheritance; the dual form of the name is taken to mean “double ornaments” or “double passages.”
biblical_def: Adithaim is a city in the lowland of Judah, listed among the fourteen towns of one cluster of the Shephelah: “And Sharaim, and Adithaim, and Gederah, and Gederothaim; fourteen cities with their villages” (Jos 15:36). It is named but once, and the story of Scripture tells nothing further of it. The form of its name is dual, and is taken to mean double ornaments or double passages — a small town of the foothills, perhaps set at a crossing of ways. Its worth to the reader lies not in any recorded deed but in its place within the exactness of the inheritance. When Joshua and Eleazar and the heads of the tribes divided the land by lot before the LORD, they left no corner uncounted; even Adithaim, of which nothing else is known, was set down in the sacred record and given to Judah. “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” (Pro 16:33). The very lots that fell for these towns fell as God appointed. So a nameless double-gated town of the valley becomes a witness to the doctrine that nothing in the portion of God’s people is left to chance: their bounds, their dwellings, their inheritance are measured out by the hand of a sovereign and faithful God.

etymology: A city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, near the vale of Elah; called Shaaraim in the narrative of David and Goliath. The dual name is taken to mean “two gates.”
biblical_def: Sharaim is a city in the lowland of Judah, named at the head of a cluster of Shephelah towns: “And Sharaim, and Adithaim, and Gederah, and Gederothaim” (Jos 15:36). Its dual name is taken to mean two gates. The same town, spelled Shaaraim, marks the line of Philistine flight after David felled Goliath in the vale of Elah: “And the wounded of the Philistines fell down by the way to Shaaraim, even unto Gath, and unto Ekron” (1Sa 17:52). Here the little two-gated town of the valley stands as a milestone of one of the great deliverances of Scripture. When the shepherd of Bethlehem went out against the giant with a sling and five smooth stones, he did it in the name of the LORD of hosts, that all the earth might know there is a God in Israel, and that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear. The rout that ran past Shaaraim was not the victory of a stronger arm but of a truer faith; the giant fell, and the road to the Philistine cities was strewn with the wounded of the enemies of God. So the road by Sharaim preaches the gospel pattern — that God delivers His people not by the might they trust, but by the weak and despised means He is pleased to bless, that the glory of the deliverance may be wholly His.

etymology: A city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, named in the roll of Judah’s inheritance; the name means “tower of Gad” or “tower of fortune,” Gad being an old word for fortune or good luck.
biblical_def: Migdal-gad is a city in the lowland of Judah, named once in the roll of Judah’s inheritance: “Zenan, and Hadashah, and Migdalgad” (Jos 15:37). The name means tower of Gad, or tower of fortune — for Gad was an old Semitic word for fortune or good luck, and became the name of a false god of fortune among the nations, whom apostate Israel later worshipped. Isaiah rebukes those who “prepare a table for that troop” (Isa 65:11), where the word rendered troop is this very Gad, the deity of luck. So the name of this little tower-town of Judah carries in it a warning stitched into the very map of the land: even in the inheritance of the LORD there stood a Tower of Fortune, a name testifying how ready the human heart is to trust in luck, fate, and fortune rather than in the living God. The believer is called to purge such idols from his speech and his hope. There is no fortune, no blind luck, no fickle fate ruling the affairs of men; there is only the sovereign, wise, and holy providence of God, who worketh all things after the counsel of His own will. The tower of Gad falls before the throne of the LORD, who alone disposeth the lot and governeth the least event.

corruption_summary: The name means “tower of fortune”; it directly rebukes the trust in luck, fate, and chance, which Scripture answers with the sovereign providence of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The very name Migdal-gad, tower of fortune, names a live and abiding corruption: the trust of the human heart in luck, fate, chance, and fortune. From the Gad of the ancient nations to the horoscopes, lucky charms, and “fingers crossed” of the present day, men have ever set up a Tower of Fortune to worship in the place of God.

Scripture will have none of it. There is no blind luck and no fickle fate; God worketh all things after the counsel of His own will (Eph 1:11), and the lot cast into the lap is wholly disposed of the LORD (Pro 16:33). The believer casts down the tower of Gad and rests in a providence that is personal, wise, holy, and sure. To say “good luck” as if fortune governed is to forget the God who numbers the hairs and rules the fall of the sparrow.

etymology: A city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, near Lachish; called Boscath in the account of King Josiah. The name is taken to mean “rocky height” or “stony ground.”
biblical_def: Bozkath is a city in the lowland of Judah, named near Lachish in the roll of Judah’s inheritance: “Lachish, and Bozkath, and Eglon” (Jos 15:39). Its lasting place in Scripture is quiet but honorable: it was the home town of the family of the godly king Josiah’s mother. “And his mother’s name was Jedidah, the daughter of Adaiah of Boscath” (2Ki 22:1). From this obscure hill-town of the valley came the mother who bore and, we may believe, helped to shape one of the most faithful kings ever to sit on David’s throne — the boy who began to reign at eight years old, and who “did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, and walked in all the way of David his father, and turned not aside to the right hand or to the left” (2Ki 22:2). Josiah tore down the high places, cleansed the temple, found the book of the law, and led Judah in a great renewal of the covenant. Behind that reformation stood, in part, a mother of Bozkath. So this town preaches the hidden, generational work of God through godly households: the LORD is pleased to raise up reformers and kings out of nameless towns and faithful mothers, weaving His purposes through the quiet fidelity of families whose names the world never learns.

etymology: A city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, named in the roll of Judah’s inheritance; the name is taken to mean “understanding” or “a mound.”
biblical_def: Cabbon is a city in the lowland of Judah, named once in the roll of Judah’s inheritance: “And Cabbon, and Lahmam, and Kithlish” (Jos 15:40). It appears among a cluster of Shephelah towns and is nowhere else mentioned, and no deed of its people is recorded. Yet, like all the towns of this long catalogue, its bare naming testifies to the faithfulness of God in keeping His oath to the fathers. The whole roll of Judah’s cities — the great and the small, the famous and the forgotten — is the ledger of a promise fulfilled: “There failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken unto the house of Israel; all came to pass” (Jos 21:45). Cabbon is one entry in that ledger. The name is taken by some to mean understanding, and it may serve the reader as a call to understanding: to read even the driest lists of Scripture with the eye of faith, and to see in every name the steadfastness of the covenant-keeping God. Nothing in the word of God is idle. The Spirit who moved holy men to write down Cabbon, Lahmam, and Kithlish had a purpose in every syllable, that the church in every age might rest upon a God who performs to the uttermost all that He has spoken.
